summaries.example: Imagine you promised to meet a friend, but on the way you see someone who needs urgent help. The promise is one reason to keep going. The person’s need is a reason to stop and help. Thinking about which reason matters more is one simple example of weighing reasons.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what it means to weigh reasons. Reasons are things that count directly in favor of an action or belief, such as keeping a promise, helping someone, or using good evidence. Weighing does not simply mean placing reasons on a literal scale. It means explaining how reasons and other background factors work together to produce judgments such as “allowed,” “required,” or “best.” The entry also distinguishes a person’s own thinking from the structure of a system like morality or careful belief. It explores whether reasons always have one fixed strength, whether situations can change them, how several reasons combine, and what happens when different systems disagree.
key_ideas: Reasons can support different choices, and those reasons may compete.
Weighing reasons is mainly about how a system, such as morality, reaches a judgment—not just about how a person thinks.
A reason can matter more or less depending on the situation.
Some choices may both be allowed, even when one seems better than the other.
Different systems, such as morality and self-interest, may give different answers.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often face choices with more than one important consideration. Understanding reasons can help us see why a choice may be allowed without being required, why a promise may matter differently in different situations, and why two people or two standards may give different guidance. It also teaches us to be careful: saying that one reason “outweighs” another is a philosophical claim that needs an explanation.

important_terms.definition: A fact or consideration that supports doing something or believing something.
A possible action or belief that can be judged as allowed, required, or better.
A way of deciding what is allowed, required, or best in a certain area, such as morality or careful thinking.
A reason that matters directly in deciding what is allowed, required, or best.
A background fact that can turn a reason on or off, such as whether a promise was freely made.

questions_to_think_about: Can two different choices both be allowed?
When should a promise stop being a reason to do something?
Is a reason always the same strength in every situation?
What should we do when morality and self-interest disagree?

summaries.example: Consider three options: keep a promise to meet a friend, remain a bystander, or save a child from a burning building at serious cost to yourself. Saving the child may be required when the only cost is breaking the promise. Avoiding serious injury may make remaining a bystander permissible when no promise exists. Yet when all three options are present, the promise can make remaining a bystander impermissible even though avoiding injury is a powerful consideration. The case raises the question of whether a reason’s force can depend on which alternative it is compared with.
summaries.summary: The entry treats weighing reasons as a theory of the internal structure of a normative perspective. A perspective takes relevant considerations as inputs and yields verdicts such as permissible, required, or supererogatory. The central task is to explain how direct reasons, contextual conditions, modifiers, and the reasons for competing options interact. One influential proposal compares each option with its alternatives, but this approach faces difficulties: moral permission appears both stable under small improvements and common in everyday life, while exact ties would be rare and fragile. Philosophers therefore consider parity, incommensurability, and weight pluralism, which distinguishes, for example, weight that supports permission from weight that supports requirement. The entry also examines contrastive reasons, the individuation of options, holism, exclusionary reasons, aggregation, and conflicts among normative perspectives. It remains neutral about whether normative weight is genuinely analogous to physical weight.
key_ideas: The entry studies the structure of normative perspectives, not primarily the psychological process by which an agent deliberates.
A full account must explain how reasons for incompatible options compete, including cases with more than two options.
Pairwise comparison is one influential model, but it faces problems involving stable and widespread moral permission.
Parity, incommensurability, and plural kinds of weight are competing ways to explain why more than one option can be permissible.
Context may enable, disable, amplify, or weaken reasons; the strongest version of this idea is particularism.
Reasons can combine in complex ways, and conflicts between morality, prudence, and epistemic rationality may lack a single final authority.
summaries.why_it_matters: The framework clarifies familiar disagreements without assuming that one side is simply irrational. It separates questions about what counts as a reason from questions about how reasons combine and from questions about which normative system has authority. These distinctions matter in ethics, epistemology, and practical reasoning because they affect whether an action is forbidden, required, optional, or better than another permitted action.

important_terms.definition: A consideration that directly contributes to a normative judgment about an action or belief.
A possible action, belief, or other response that is being evaluated.
A system that produces normative verdicts, such as morality, prudence, etiquette, or epistemic rationality.
The degree to which a reason directly matters within a normative perspective.
A view that an option is permissible when its reasons are not outweighed by the reasons for any alternative.
A reason whose applicability or strength changes depending on the alternative against which it is compared.
The view that a feature can change from being a reason, or can change its direction or strength, depending on context.
A view that different kinds of weight may perform different normative jobs, such as making an option permissible versus making it required.

questions_to_think_about: Does a reason have one fixed weight, or can its force depend on the comparison being made?
Can an option be permissible even when another permissible option is morally better?
Would a theory of reasons need to consider only the most fully specified options?
Are conditions and modifiers genuinely different from reasons?
If normative perspectives conflict, must there be a supreme perspective to settle the conflict?

summaries.example: Suppose you are choosing between joining a sports team and joining a music club. You have reasons for each: friends may be on the team, while the music club may fit your interests better. Now add a school rule, a promise to help with one activity, or a special circumstance at home. These extra facts might not be new reasons by themselves. They could change whether an earlier reason applies or how strongly it counts. A philosopher studying weighing reasons asks how these parts should work together and whether either choice can still be perfectly acceptable.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates how reasons support actions and beliefs. A reason might be a promise, a benefit, a right, an experience, or evidence. To weigh reasons is to explain how these considerations interact inside a standard such as morality or epistemic rationality. The topic is not mainly about the mental steps a person uses while deciding; it is about the structure that connects relevant factors to judgments like permissible, required, or best. The entry considers several disagreements. Some theories compare an option with each alternative. Others allow contrastive reasons, whose strength depends on the comparison. Philosophers also debate whether choices can be on a par rather than exactly tied, whether reasons have different kinds of weight, and whether context can change a reason. Finally, the entry asks how reasons combine and what happens when different standards conflict.
key_ideas: Weighing reasons is not literally using a balance scale; it is a theory about how considerations lead to judgments.
A person deciding what to do and a moral system judging what is allowed are related but different topics.
Reasons can point toward different options, and there may be more than two options.
Some philosophers think two reasons can be neither exactly equal nor clearly stronger; this relation is sometimes called parity.
Context can change whether a reason exists or how strong it is.
Morality, self-interest, and evidence may sometimes give different guidance.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps explain why real decisions are not always simple contests between one good thing and one bad thing. It shows why a choice can be allowed without being the best choice, why circumstances can change the meaning of a fact, and why different standards may disagree. Studying these ideas builds careful thinking about both moral choices and beliefs based on evidence.

important_terms.definition: Something that counts in favor of an action or belief.
One of the alternatives being judged, such as an action or a belief.
A standard or point of view that gives judgments about what is allowed, required, or best.
How strongly a reason counts within that point of view.
A background circumstance that can make a reason apply or stop applying.
A circumstance that changes the strength of a reason without turning it completely on or off.
A reason whose force changes when the comparison option changes.
The idea that the same feature may matter differently in different situations.

questions_to_think_about: Could two choices both be acceptable even if one seems better?
Can a promise stop counting if it was made under pressure?
Should a reason against one option count as a reason for every other option?
Why might a choice look different when there are three options instead of two?
What should happen when moral advice conflicts with advice about self-interest?
